entries.title: Dutch police disperse violent far-right protest in The Hague
entries.summary: After violence broke out, Dutch riot police dispersed hundreds of far-right protesters in The Hague. Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that the demonstrators had chanted "abhorrent" far-right and antisemitic slogans.
entries.content:
Netherlands

Dutch police disperse violent far-right protest in The Hague

September 20, 2026

After violence broke out, Dutch riot police dispersed hundreds of far-right protesters in The Hague. Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that the demonstrators had chanted "abhorrent" far-right and antisemitic slogans.

Dutch riot police on Saturday clashed with approximately 500 far-right protesters who chanted antisemitic slogans at a rally in The Hague city center.

The protesters threw fireworks and other projectiles at the police.

According to AFP reporters on the scene, police used baton charges and specialist dogs to break up the demonstration.

What do we know about the protest

The "We Are the People" rally was organized to protest government policies, particularly those related to immigration.

Protesters had planned to march through the city, but local authorities banned the march when violence broke out in the park where protesters were gathering. Authorities then ordered the demonstration to break up.

The police said that they arrested 24 people and used water cannons to disperse the rioters. They added that further investigations are underway.

How did the authorities react

On X, Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that the demonstrators had deliberately sought confrontation with the police and had chanted "abhorrent" far-right and antisemitic slogans.

Meanwhile, Justice Minister David van Weel called for an "extremely firm" response to the "disgusting scenes" that occurred at the protest.

Van Weel said demonstrators made Nazi salutes, chanted antisemitic slogans, attacked police, and threw fireworks at riot officers.

Saturday's unrest occurred one year after riots broke out during a right-wing demonstration.

During clashes between black-clad protesters and police, a police car was set on fire, and the headquarters of the centrist D66 party — whose leader, Rob Jetten, is now prime minister — was attacked.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Summer of 2026 broke records in Europe, and caused deaths
entries.summary: The summer of 2026 was not only the hottest on record in Europe, it also saw a record number of people die. More than 16,000 are thought to have died because of the heat in Germany alone.
entries.content:
September 19, 2026

The summer of 2026 was not only the hottest on record in Europe, it also saw a record number of people die. More than 16,000 are thought to have died because of the heat in Germany alone.

The summer (June to August) of 2026 was the warmest in Europe since records began, beating the record set in 2003, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service,

Not only that, Germany's DWD weather service says that there was an "unprecedented" number of hot days this year. "On average across Germany,there were about 22 hot days with temperatures of at least 30 degrees Celsius and about five very hot days with temperatures of at least 35 degrees Celsius," the DWD wrote in in a press release at the end of August.

The estimated number of heat-related deaths also reached unprecedented levels, with at least 16,300 people dying by the end of August, even if few of them died directly because of the heat, but rather as a consequence of underlying health conditions exacerbated by the heat.

The figures were compiled from a statistical correlation between the number of deaths recorded by Germany's Federal Statistical Office and the temperatures measured by the DWD during a specific period.

Heat-related deaths in Germany are more likely if the average weekly temperature reaches 20 degrees Celsius or more. This is the average of all hourly temperatures recorded in a week, including at nighttime.

This year, the average weekly temperatures in the country rose above the 20-degree mark several times. It was particularly hot at the end of June, when the average weekly temperature reached above 26 degrees between the 22nd and 28th of the month.

Excess mortality during heat waves

Though it is not possible to determine a cause of death using statistics, researchers and medical professionals have a good understanding of how heat affects the human body, and there is widespread consensus that excess mortality during heat waves is possible.

"It was not just the high temperatures on the thermometer that were important, but also how long the heat lasted and the fact that it hardly cooled down at night," said Andreas Matzarakis, professor of environmental meteorology at Freiburg University.

Many people have trouble sleeping on hot nights. Yet, getting enough sleep is important so that the body can recover from the heat and stress of the day.

Matzarakis said that the severity of heat stress was not related solely to air temperatures. Humidity, solar radiation and wind also played a role — and what is known as the 'felt' temperature. He said that humidity and still air could place a heavy strain on the body, even in moderate temperatures.

Underprivileged most vulnerable

The less privileged members of society were also among the most vulnerable, said Martin Röösli, environmental scientist at the Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute in Basel. "They are more likely to live in homes that are not well insulated or are more likely to work outdoors."

A large proportion of those who died because of the heat probably had only a short life expectancy left, due to their age and medical conditions, but Röösli said that there was a consensus that "some of the deceased could have lived for a long time and were simply in a fragile state at the time of the heat wave."

For Alexandra Schneider, a meteorologist and epidemiologist at the Helmholtz center in Munich in southern Germany, the deaths that occurred during the heat waves were very likely not only because of the "harvesting effect," which describes "how a heat wave causes very vulnerable individuals in particular to die a few days or weeks prematurely."

Had this been the case, there would have been a deficit of mortality in the following weeks, which did not happen. Thus, she believes, a significant proportion of those who died could have lived on for months or even years.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Trump announces new 'AI force' amid mounting pressure
entries.summary: Several voices, including from within the AI industry, have been calling for policing the fast-growing technology. Trump has once again called AI warnings "hoaxes" and vowed to "cherish, help" the industry.
entries.content:
September 19, 2026

Several voices, including from within the AI industry, have been calling for policing the fast-growing technology. Trump has once again called AI warnings "hoaxes" and vowed to "cherish, help" the industry.

US President Donald Trump has said he is forming an "AI force," as many, including those from within the industry, have recently sounded the alarm about the dangers of Artificial Intelligence continuing to grow unchecked.

In a social media post on Saturday, Trump said he will announce an "AI czar" to lead the force soon.

The US president continued to brush off warnings about AI's dangers from experts and the AI industry itself as "hoaxes" pushed by the Democrats.

What did Trump say about the 'AI force'?

While dismissing warnings about AI, Trump still vowed to be "be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing criminal and civil justice system."

"For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my first term. To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI 'Czar,'" Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

The US president, who has enjoyed a close relationship with big tech bosses especially during his second term in office, also vowed "not in any way hinder or stifle the growth of this incredible Industry," in reference to AI.

"Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!"

He described AI as "the next industrial revolution," predicting it will account for 25% of the US GDP.

"We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!"

Trump compared the criticism of the unchecked, ultrafast growth of AI to what he called other "hoaxes," listing efforts to impeach him, transgender rights and global warming as examples.

Why have there been growing calls for regulating AI?

Some of the top names in AI said earlier this week they were working on creating a standards body they say would regulate the industry.

Industry giants including ChatGPT's OpenAI, Google and Anthropic said they envisioned a self-regulatory body.

The proposal comes amid growing concerns about AI safety, which have escelated in recent weeks, with several AI agents going rogue and breaking into competitors' systems.

Even top names within the industry have raised similar concerns.

Last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slowdown in the industry's development, with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, xAI's Elon Musk and Google DeepMind chair Demis Hassabis all supporting the sentiment.

Trump has dismissed calls to contain AI development as "hoaxes" and a "conspiracy."

Smaller AI companies have meanwhile warned any self-regulatory measures spearheaded by the big names would come at their expense.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: German-Russian relations at freezing point
entries.summary: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine destroyed the once-close relationship between Moscow and Berlin. Yet the far-right AfD is calling for a normalization of relations.
entries.content:
Germany

German-Russian relations at freezing point

September 19, 2026

Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine destroyed the once-close relationship between Moscow and Berlin. Yet the far-right AfD is calling for a normalization of relations.

For many years, Germany and Russia had a perfect partnership.

Russia supplied cheap energy, which helped German industry succeed in exporting its goods worldwide. This partnership began in the early 2000s. On the German side was Chancellor Gerhard Schröder from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), followed later by Chancellor Angela Merkel of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Their counterpart was Vladimir Putin.

Even when Russia annexed the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea in 2014, business continued as usual. It was then that the agreement to build Nord Stream 2, a direct gas pipeline between Russia and Germany designed to bypass Ukraine was signed. At the time, other European countries and the US warned that the pipeline would provide Russia with powerful leverage.

The warnings proved to be correct. On February 24, 2022, Russian tanks rolled into Ukraine. German hopes for a stable European order, the democratization of Russia, and the continuation of its lucrative business model were shattered.

How could so many German politicians be so wrong?

"Shortly before the invasion, the widespread view was that there were no rational grounds for an attack on Ukraine, because the economic, military, and political costs to Russia of starting a war would be far too high," Russia expert Mario Baumann of the German Council on Foreign Relations told DW. "People [in Germany] had projected their own rationality onto Russia. They underestimated the regime's imperialist and revisionist ambitions."

After that, nothing in the bilateral relationship was ever the same again. Chancellor Olaf Scholz(SPD) spoke of a Zeitenwende (epochal shift) in foreign and security policy, in the days after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine began.

Since then, the German armed forces have expanded. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said the following year, "We must become capable of waging war," a statement that critics still say was an escalation of tensions.

Germany ended its decades-long energy dependence on Russia and shut down Nord Stream 2. In September 2022, the pipeline was blown up. The Federal Prosecutor's Office suspects a Ukrainian group was responsible.

A series of EU sanctions have long since reduced Russian-German trade relations to a minimum. Government cooperation in culture, science, and education has also practically ceased to exist.

A new low point

While the German government under Scholz initially hesitated to take dramatic steps on military aid to Ukraine, Friedrich Merz, then the leader of the opposition, stepped up his rhetoric.

"Ukraine must win the war. Russia must lose the war," he said in 2024 as leader of the CDU/CSU parliamentary group in parliament. In 2025, as chancellor, he then spoke of Russia's "economic exhaustion," which the West must "help bring about." But that has yet to materialize. To this day, Russia has shown no serious willingness to compromise.

Meanwhile, Germany is feeling the consequences of its military support for Ukraine. The German government has long suspected Russia of being behind cyberattacks on government agencies and critical infrastructure.

So when an armed drone was discovered and defused in August 2026 at Leipzig Airport close to Ukrainian transport aircraft — which transport a large portion of the military aid to Ukraine — the government was certain: For the first time, it publicly blamed the Kremlin.

A Russian cultural center in Berlin and the Russian consulate in Bonn were closed, which the German government said were being used as espionage centers. Moscow responded by closing the Goethe Institutes and the German consulate in St. Petersburg.

Putin has denied Russian responsibility for the Leipzig incident, calling it a "serious mistake" to blame Moscow, while Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov even described the accusations as the "beginning of a real war." But Baumann says: "We shouldn't give in to the fears being stoked, because they are part of Russia's strategy to weaken Germany and Europe."

AfD wants to resume relations with Russia

The German government is also facing domestic pressure as the far-right Alternative for Germany(AfD) has made gains in regional elections and is rising in the national polls. The AfD would prefer to end support for Ukraine and normalize relations with Russia, including deals on oil and gas. High fuel prices in Germany have only made the issue more explosive.

"German support for Ukraine worries many people," said Sven Leunig, political scientist at the University of Jena in Thuringia, following the election in the neighboring state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won the September 6 election by a landslide. However, he noted, "it is less a fundamental rejection of the support itself than a reaction born of fear. People want to 'stay out' of the conflict so as not to be drawn into it more deeply themselves."

In the latest ARD Deutschlandtrend survey, 42% of respondents believe military aid to Ukraine has gone too far. "If public support weakens over the long term, the government will eventually have to respond," says Leunig.

Carry on or change course?

So far, the German government is sticking to its course, as Merz made clear once again following the AfD's election victory. But opinions on how to deal with Russia and the war in Ukraine differ not only among politicians but also among political scientists and experts.

Johannes Varwick of Halle University in Saxony-Anhalt believes it is long past time for a change of course: "German and European policy toward Ukraine resembles a mix of platitudes and wishful thinking," Varwick told DW. "It is high time for a course correction, and Germany should exert pressure on Ukraine to move closer to the latest American proposals, which aim for a compromise and could thus possibly bring about a political solution."

Baumann, on the other hand, argues: "Supporting Ukraine remains the best investment for safeguarding German and European interests. The government has recognized this and should stick to this course and continue to communicate it as such." However, it is important that Berlin act in concert with its European partners.

The war in Ukraine has now lasted longer than World War I. And there is no end in sight. Hopes that Russian-German relations will return to the way they used to be seem illusory for the foreseeable future.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Ukraine steps up measures to protect railways
entries.summary: As Russia increases its attacks on Ukraine's rail infrastructure, the Ukrainian government has called for help to replace destroyed locomotives and is making plans to keep passengers safe.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine steps up measures to protect railways

September 19, 2026

As Russia increases its attacks on Ukraine's rail infrastructure, the Ukrainian government has called for help to replace destroyed locomotives and is making plans to keep passengers safe.

Recent months have seen a rise in Russian drone attacks on locomotives, stations, and infrastructure. More than 1,600 attacks were reported in the first eight months of 2026, according to Oleh Holovashchenko from Ukrzaliznytsia, the state rail operator.

On September 16, a train traveling between the capital Kyiv and Mykolaiv in southern Ukraine was struck by a Russian drone. The day before, another train in the Volhynia region was attacked near the Polish border.

Two days earlier, a drone had struck the locomotive of a passenger train at the Yahodyn border crossing, just two kilometers (1.2 miles) from Polish territory. Nobody was injured, as Ukrzaliznytsia's monitoring system had previously detected the drone and the train had been evacuated about 15 minutes before the attack. At the time, CIA Director David Petraeus was on another train at the same station.

A separate train carrying several former European leaders, including ex-British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and security advisers had stopped at the station earlier the same day. The Ukrainian authorities believe that this diplomatic train was the drone's actual target, but the train departed earlier than scheduled.

'Putin's terror' against Ukrainian logistics

Russia has damaged or destroyed more than 500 Ukrainian locomotives since its full-scale invasion of Ukrainebegan in 2022. More than half of these attacks happened this year, according to a post on the social media platform X by Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha. He said that part of "Putin's terror" was to destabilize Ukraine's logistics system.

The minister called on international partners to tighten sanctions against Russia further and to provide financial assistance to the Ukrainian government so that it can procure more locomotives that are compatible with Ukraine's Soviet-era broad-gauge (1,520 millimeters or almost 5 feet).

"Ukraine's railway keeps the country moving," Sybiha said. "It enables the rapid evacuation of civilians from frontline areas, transports essential cargo, and keeps grain and other critical goods moving across the country."

Russia was specifically targeting locomotives because they were ideal from a technical point of view, said Vasyl Shevchenko, a former Ukrainian deputy transport minister. "A locomotive's thermal signature is very large, and almost impossible to miss," he told DW. "The impact of a strike can be devastating, because 50 kilograms (110 pounds) of explosives in a diesel locomotive can cause several metric tons of fuel to detonate and completely destroy it. A strike on an electric locomotive will cause a fire that can paralyze an entire stretch of track. That's why they are targeting areas where the loss of a single train can bring traffic to a standstill."

Shevchenko also pointed out that locomotives could not be replaced immediately but had to be ordered in advance and this could take years. Ukrzaliznytsia says that negotiations are underway with various international partners and a contract has already been signed with the French company Alstom. These locomotives are scheduled to start arriving next year.

In the meantime, trains are also being repaired. "While our top priorities used to be saving on costs, providing comfort to the train crew and making sure the trains were attractive, these have changed," Holovashchenko said. "What is most important today is that the locomotive is technically sound and ready to transport passengers and freight." But he added that it was difficult to protect trains against Russia's weapons.

Zelenskyy intensifies protection of critical infrastructure

On September 15, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held a meeting of the staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief to discuss strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure and logistics.

The key issues were contracts for the production of protection systems for critical infrastructure and logistics, but he added that there were plans to expand the electronic warfare component and reorganize the operation of designated mobile fire teams, as well as strengthening air defense lines.

Zelenskyy said that decisions on backup logistics routes in frontline regions were also being made, and he had instructed Ukraine's Finance Ministry of to find additional funding for the logistics sector.

Ukrzaliznytsia sets up monitoring centers

According to Holovashchenko, Ukrzaliznytsia is also seeking its own answers to the new challenges and there are plans to develop early detection systems. He said that a monitoring center had been established to track the movement of drones and trains all over Ukraine.

The fact that Russia has started to use jet-powered Shahed-type drones, which are much faster than previous models, has made it more difficult and given less time to respond. "We used to wait longer to stop trains so we could evacuate passengers," Holovashchenko said. "Now, there are more precautionary stops. But in general, we try not to go into areas where there is a potential danger."

Buses are deployed in areas of particularly high risk and the "train plus bus" concept is being expanded in cooperation with military authorities. Passengers are also being given instructions on how to respond in the event of an alarm and advised to try to get further away from a station than previously.

The most difficult question remains where they should be evacuated to. Holovashchenko said that the monitoring centers had access to maps showing all the shelters along train routes and that dispatchers always tried to stop trains near them, but this was not always possible. He said that train personnel were receiving special psychological support to help passengers.

Ukrzaliznytsia is currently preparing for winter, while working with foundations and other donors to ensure that trains will be heated. Evacuations will be even more difficult as temperatures drop. "This is no easy task. We're providing blankets, rain jackets, and equipment so that train staff can supply passengers with at least the bare necessities if their train comes to a standstill in the middle of nowhere because of a snowstorm, Holovashchenko said.

This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

entries.title: CNN, MS NOW and Politico denied access to White House
entries.summary: Three US news outlets said their journalists were blocked from entering the White House grounds, hours after President Donald Trump announced bans on several media outlets.
entries.content:
September 19, 2026

Three US news outlets said their journalists were blocked from entering the White House grounds, hours after President Donald Trump announced bans on several media outlets.

News outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Saturday signaled they would take legal action after their journalists were denied access to the White House grounds earlier in the day.

It comes a day after US President Donald Trump announced he would ban the three news outlets from 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue in a row over their coverage of his presidency.

Trump has accused the media of "fake news" over their often critical coverage of his second term in office.

Experts say the bans conflict with the United States Constitution's First Amendment protections for free speech and press freedom.

What did CNN, MS NOW and Politico say?

CNN reported that its journalist Betsy Klein was denied access at the White House on Saturday morning and her press pass was seized.

"CNN’s mission to report on the U.S. government will continue regardless of any attempts to restrict physical access to the White House and other government buildings, or any other attempts to impede our journalism,” a statement from the channel said.

“We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right."

Meanwhile, the left-leaning MS NOW, whose journalists were also turned away from the White House grounds on Saturday, said in a statement that it would challenge Trump's ban.

"The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars,” the network said. "MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy.”

Politico's global editor-in-chief Jonathan Greenberger, meanwhile, wrote in an email to staff that reporter Cheyenne Haslett was denied entry to White House and her pass was confiscated by the Secret Service.

"We stand by her and all reporters here covering the White House. As we said yesterday, we will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights."

Jacqui Heinrich, President of the White House Correspondents' Association, warned that Trump's ban would "extend beyond these organizations," warning that it "could be applied to any outlet in the future."

Heinrich urged the Trump administration "to immediately restore our colleagues’ access."

What did Trump accuse US media outlets of?

In a post on his Truth Social network, Trump said the media outlets "shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the president of the United States."

"Other fake news media outlets to follow," he warned.

Trump said there was no one incident that prompted the ban, telling reporters in the Oval Office, "It's really just cumulative stories over the past few years."

"I don't have to let them into my, into the people's house," he added.

It was unclear whether the banned media outlets would also be blocked from flights aboard the presidential plane, Air Force One.

The US is just weeks away from the November 3 midterm elections in which Trump's Republican Party will struggle to defend narrow majorities in Congress.

With the president's approval ratings at 35%, near historic lows, Reuters/Ipsos polls also show Democrats ahead by around 7-9 points.

Trump's war with the press

During his second term, Trump has continued to round on journalists he deems critical to his administration — a tactic he employed when first elected in 2016.

Last year, he banned the Associated Press news agency from the usual pool of journalists that report on the presidency over its refusal to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.

He has, however, given closer access to new, far-right media outlets seen as more sympathetic to his policies.

Trump has even called on the US media regulator to remove the licenses of several broadcasters, whose comedy or news shows have mocked his policies and family.

The president has also filed several lawsuits against the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times, the BBC and Iowa's Des Moines Register, sometimes costing the media outlets millions in settlements.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania: Will economy shape the vote?
entries.summary: Voters in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania head to the polls on Sunday, with the Social Democrats and far-right AfD neck and neck. Here's a look at key economic issues that could influence the election.
entries.content:
September 19, 2026

Voters in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania head to the polls on Sunday, with the Social Democrats and far-right AfD neck and neck. Here's a look at key economic issues that could influence the election.

The recent election victory of the far-right AfD party in Saxony-Anhalt has shaken up Germany's political landscape. Although Saxony-Anhalt is only a small state, the AfD's landslide win with nearly 44% of the vote has drawn considerable international attention, as it means this would the first time that a far-right party will likely enter a German government since World War II.

That is not expected to happen in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where voters head to the ballot box on Sunday. State Premier Manuela Schwesig of the center-left Social Democrats remains popular, as polls show, though she isn't without her critics.

The latest polls suggest a neck-and-neck race between the Social Democrats and AfD, rather than a landslide victory for any one party. In fact, the Social Democrats' approval ratings have been on the rise and could indicate a successful final push, potentially returning Schwesig to power.

Lower wages, but solid economic growth

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, like Saxony-Anhalt, is in eastern Germany, but its economy is relatively stable, even though unemployment stands at 7.8%, slightly above the national average, and the median gross annual salary is €47,750 ($54,800) — about €6,000 less than the German average. But Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has seen solid economic growth in recent years.

Jochen Schulte, state secretary in the state's Economy Ministry, said Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania's economy has expanded by 5% in inflation-adjusted terms since 2020, compared with 4.6% for Germany overall.

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has a large agricultural sector, although it employs relatively few people. Back when the state was part of East Germany, farms were consolidated into large, state-run enterprises known as agricultural production cooperatives, rather than privately organized as in West Germany.

In many instances, these farm sizes have remained the same since reunification. A typical agricultural company in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will control about 280 to 283 hectares (up to 700 acres) of land, whereas the national average is only about 65 hectares.

The state's now private agricultural companies continue to benefit from their large size, ensuring efficient labor use, strong market positioning, greater market power through centralized purchasing, and a strong negotiating position when selling produce.

Many jobs in shipbuilding, tourism

The state's second major industry is shipbuilding and maritime services, which accounts for a significant share of economic output. Being on Germany's Baltic Sea coast, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has also benefited from the recent investment boom in its defense sector. This has brought business — and jobs — to major shipyards in Wismar and Stralsund, at companies like Thyssenkrupp Marine Systems and other shipbuilders.

Tourism is another key sector in the state. Until 1990, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania was one of the most important travel destinations for East Germans. Since the fall of the Berlin Wall, Germans from east and west have continued to flock to the Baltic coast, and the region is Germany's second-most popular vacation destination.

That said, relatively few people are directly employed in the tourism sector. That is in part merely a statistical quirk, as many tourism jobs overlapping with service jobs, and also because many tourism jobs are seasonal.

According to figures from the Economy Ministry and industry reports, some 150,000 to 160,000 jobs depend on tourism, either directly or indirectly. Water-based tourism, whether on lakes or the Baltic Sea coast, accounts for an estimated 19,000 jobs.

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has few large enterprises, such as automakers and chemical companies, which makes its state and civil service branch the region's largest employer.

Rostock-based AIDA Cruises is another major employer. So is Nordex SE, a manufacturer of wind turbines with production facilities in various regions. German rail operator Deutsche Bahn provides many jobs through its service and maintenance hubs, as do the major ports of Rostock and Sassnitz.

Fossil fuels, renewables power regional economy

Another key industry is the energy sector, with large quantities of Germany's fossil fuels brought in via the Baltic Sea.

When imports of Russian gas came to a standstill in 2022 following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Nord Stream gas pipeline connection points near Lubmin lost their significance. However, a large portion of Germany's liquefied natural gas imports are still unloaded, processed and distributed in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

Energy availability, not only from fossil fuels such as oil and gas, but also from green sources such as wind and solar power, is becoming increasingly important for the state as well.

In August, the Schwarz Group — which operates the Lidl and Kaufland supermarket chains — announced it would invest €5.6 billion ($6.4 billion) in the construction of a data center south of Rostock.

During the project's presentation in the state capital, Schwerin, the company said its investments in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania could reach tens of billions of euros.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Saudi Arabia: Houthis claim strikes on Riyadh, Yanbu port
entries.summary: The Yemen-based Houthis said they targeted "sensitive sites" in Riyadh, hours after a blaze at a fuel depot near the Saudi capital's main airport. The Saudi-led coalition said Saudi defense downed a ballistic missile.
entries.content:
Saudi Arabia

Saudi Arabia: Houthis claim strikes on Riyadh, Yanbu port

September 19, 2026

The Yemen-based Houthis said they targeted "sensitive sites" in Riyadh, hours after a blaze at a fuel depot near the Saudi capital's main airport. The Saudi-led coalition said Saudi defense downed a ballistic missile.

Yemen-based Houthi rebels said they targeted "sensitive sites" in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and oil facilities in the port city of Yanbu on Saturday.

A statement posted to Telegram from the Iran-backed group came hours after firefighters extinguished a blaze at a fuel depot near King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital.

Earlier, residents reported hearing explosions in the vicinity, following overnight warnings by Saudi authorities of a "hostile aerial threat."

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said in a statement on X that Saudi defense forces intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched toward Riyadh in the early hours of Saturday.

A statement from the coalition's spokesman described the latest attack as "terrorist and aggressive behavior," accusing the Houthi rebels of attempting to target civilians.

What did the Houthis say?

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the rebels had "carried out two successful military operations using a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones."

Saree continued: "The first targeted sensitive sites in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, and the second targeted Aramco facilities in Yanbu."

He said the attacks were in retaliation for recent Saudi attacks on the Yemeni capital Sanaa.

The fresh violence comes just days after Riyadh accused the Houthis of targeting the Holy city of Mecca, which the Iran-backed militants denied as a "worn-out lie."

What do we know about the airport strike?

AFP journalists then reported hearing two explosions before the Saudi civil defence agency lifted the alert half an hour later.

"The area is under a hostile aerial threat," a message sent to Riyadh residents warned overnight, urging them to stay indoors, AFP news agency reported.

News agency Reuters later published video and photos of a large plume of black smoke rising from an area near a highway to the airport.

Saudi authorities also reported intercepting incoming Houthi missiles and drones.

Tracking website FlightRadar24 reported "major problems" at the King Khalid International Airport, listing it under its maximum disruption index.

Unravelling security situation

The latest developments come amid an escalation between the Houthisand the internationally recognized government in Yemen that is supported by Saudi Arabia.

A 2022 truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia fell apart in July after the rebels allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which defied the Saudis' control over Yemeni airspace.

As a result of the escalation, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia.

The group has reported dozens of Saudi strikes since its recent offensive to secure control over the coastal areas near the Red Sea's Bab al-Mandeb Strait — a vital global shipping route — from government hands.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Drone sightings briefly shut Luxembourg airport
entries.summary: Flights were diverted and hundreds of passengers affected after unauthorized drones appeared near Luxembourg's only international airport.
entries.content:
September 19, 2026

Flights were diverted and hundreds of passengers affected after unauthorized drones appeared near Luxembourg's only international airport.

Luxembourg authorities are investigating drone sightings that forced the country's main airport to temporarily suspend flights overnight, Prime Minister Luc Frieden said on Saturday.

Frieden said Luxembourg was working with its NATO allies following the incident, which comes amid heightened European concern over suspected hybrid attacks linked to Russia.

What happened at Luxembourg airport?

National carrier Luxair said more than 1,800 passengers were affected, with 17 incoming flights diverted to airports including Brussels, Paris and Frankfurt.

Flights resumed on Saturday, although Luxair warned that delays and knock-on disruption could continue.

The airport said the closure was a precautionary measure to protect passengers, airline crews, airport employees and aircraft.

Frieden stressed that it was too early to determine who was responsible.

"We are analyzing the situation," Frieden told a televised press conference after an emergency meeting with the country's defense and interior ministers.

Have other drones been spotted?

Frieden said "potentially larger drones" had also been observed in Luxembourg's airspace in recent days.

"This is new for Luxembourg, but it is not completely new for our neighboring countries," he said.

Unauthorized drones have previously been detected near sensitive sites elsewhere in Europe, including Belgium, Germany and Denmark.

"We will ensure, together with our partners, that we can guarantee the security of our populations," Frieden said.

European governments have repeatedly warned of Russian-linked hybrid activities since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Such incidents have included suspected sabotage, cyberattacks and unauthorized drone flights.

There is currently no evidence establishing who was responsible for the Luxembourg sightings.

Edited by: Zac Crellin

entries.title: Thousands protest Kennedy Center demolition fears
entries.summary: Protesters took part in a "Hands Around the Kennedy Center" human chain. The demonstration comes amid fears the Trump administration could tear the arts hub down.
entries.content:
United States of America

Thousands protest Kennedy Center demolition fears

September 19, 2026

Protesters took part in a "Hands Around the Kennedy Center" human chain. The demonstration comes amid fears the Trump administration could tear the arts hub down.

Thousands of people have demonstrated at the Kennedy Center in Washington D.C. amid fears President Donald Trump's administration could demolish the arts hub.

Crowds of people gathered in the Foggy Bottom area of the US capital city, many carrying signs as they joined in "Hands Around the Kennedy Center."

Some of those gathered held hands and formed a human chain around the center.

Protesters waved placards reading "hands off Kennedy Center" and sang songs close to where workers removed Trump's name from the building in June following a court order.

Protesters, residents condemn move to demolish Kennedy Center

"It makes me sick to my stomach," the AFP news agency quoted Neal Racioppo, a Washington resident who runs marketing and communications for a theatre, as saying.

Trump "can't get his name on this cherished building, so he is depriving the world of what it could be."

"He does not have a right to decide that an institution, a living memorial to a past president, can be demolished," another protester told AFP.

"The Kennedy Center is vital to the arts in Washington. We need it. We need this,” said local arts community member Bud Wilkinson.

"This is not just about putting the president's name on the Kennedy Center. It's about censoring the performances and the programming," Wilkinson said.

Trump and the Kennedy Center

The Kennedy Center — inaugurated in 1971 following the assassination of US President John F. Kennedy — has been a focal point of Trump's plans for Washington since 2025.

Trump has been pushing for major renovations and claims the building was left in a severe state of disrepair by those previously in control.

Trump's handpicked Kennedy Center board voted last year to rename the institution the Trump-Kennedy Center.

In May, a judge ruled that his name was illegally added and ordered it removed.

What has Trump said about the Kennedy Center?

On Wednesday, Trump appeared to imply that the Kennedy Center could be torn down if his administration did not receive "recognition."

"For the Trump administration, for me to get involved and to take that on long term and to carry it or to raise money to carry it, I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition, because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close," Trump said.

"It'll end up being ripped down. It's in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape," Trump told reporters.

Edited by: Karl Sexton
